newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen focusing on retail data.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen focusing on retail data.

text.p: Wall Street is expected to focus at its Tuesday opening on April retail sales data as a sign of whether the central bank will raise interest rates.
Analysts said the data, scheduled for release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, will provide direction ahead of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meeting May 20.

"If (the data are) way above estimates, it's going to be important because that would mean that for the (Federal Reserve) there is irrational exuberance in other places than the stock market," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
A consensus estimate by economists calls for a 0.3 percent drop in April retail sales overall. Excluding automobiles, sales are estimated to rise 0.1 percent.
The data are the first in a raft of economic figures out this week expected to guide the Federal Reserve in its rate decision.
Brown said he expected a mixed opening and perhaps some profit-taking after the recent strong rise in the New York markets.
Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said he expected a slightly higher opening, based on rises in European markets and in the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index.

"If it (the data) comes in stronger than expected, everything will be put aside," he said. "If that comes in copacetic, it then becomes a question of whether we can maintain this" rise driven by blue-chip stocks.
Tokyo's 225-share Nikkei average fell 14.4 points or 0.07 percent to 20,129.11.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 36.5 at 4706.1.
U.S. stocks were firmer in London, led by International Business Machines Corp. It was boosted by a buy recommendation from Goldman Sachs.
The dollar was steady against the yen in Tokyo at 119.30/40 and against the mark in Europe at 1.7010/20.
The U.S. Treasury 30-year bond was up 2/32 to yield 6.88 and the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was off 0.35 to 841.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column reported that British utility shares, shocked by a plan to tax windfall profits, are bouncing back. Some investors are betting fears are overblown.
The New York Times Market Place column said the merger of Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness Plc meant the liquor industry may wind up on a big merger spree.
